record.paper_title: Conferences WORDS, years 1997-2017: Open Problems and Conjectures
record.original_question: Do there exist infinite additive-cube-free words over the alphabets {0,1,2,3}, {0,1,4}, and {0,2,5}?

evidence.quote: Are there infinite additive-cube-free words on the following alphabets:{0, 1, 2, 3},{0, 1, 4} and{0, 2, 5}?

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Let an alphabet $A\subset\mathbb{Z}$ be a finite set of integers. A finite word $w=a_1a_2\cdots a_{3n}$ over $A$ (with $n\geq 1$) is called an additive cube if it can be split into three consecutive blocks of equal length whose digit sums are all equal, that is,
$$\sum_{i=1}^{n} a_i \;=\; \sum_{i=n+1}^{2n} a_i \;=\; \sum_{i=2n+1}^{3n} a_i.$$
An infinite word $\mathbf{w}=a_1a_2a_3\cdots\in A^{\mathbb{N}}$ is called additive-cube-free if no factor (contiguous subword) of $\mathbf{w}$ is an additive cube.

Determine, for each of the following three alphabets, whether there exists an infinite additive-cube-free word over it:
(i) $A=\{0,1,2,3\}$;
(ii) $A=\{0,1,4\}$;
(iii) $A=\{0,2,5\}$.
artifact.status_search_result: For the alphabet {0,1,2,3}, Lietard and Rosenfeld (extending work of Cassaigne, Currie, Schaeffer, and Shallit on {0,1,3,4}) established the existence of an infinite additive-cube-free word, in fact over every subset of {0,1,2,3}. For the alphabets {0,1,4} and {0,2,5}, the question is reported as still open: Rao constructed infinite additive-cube-free words over some size-3 integer alphabets such as {0,1,5}, {0,3,7}, {0,2,9}, but {0,1,4} and {0,2,5} remain among the unresolved cases.

status_evidence.title: Avoiding Additive Powers in Words (J. Andrade thesis)
status_evidence.snippet: It is still unknown if infinite additive cube-free words exist over the alphabets {0,1,2}, {0,1,3}, {0,1,4}, and {0,2,5}. Rao showed infinite additive cube-free words exist over alphabets of size 3 including {0,1,5}, {0,3,7}, {0,2,9}.

status_evidence.title: Avoidability of Additive Cubes over Alphabets of Four Numbers
status_evidence.snippet: There is an infinite additive cube-free word over every subset of {0,1,2,3}, extending Cassaigne–Currie–Schaeffer–Shallit's result on {0,1,3,4}.
